title: Companies Are Fighting Over College Freshmen. Phone Makers Try Hardest, but State-Owned Firms Get Special Access
body:
## Commerce is reshaping the so-called "ivory tower," because students are important young consumers. And yes, merchants don't want to lose at the starting line either.

Regular article

On her way to registration, Lu Wenwen, a new student at the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, was handed more than 10 flyers, a hand fan, a deck of playing cards and a card holder.

Merchants' stalls filled the campus. Tents of every color took over the main road, and trampled flyers and ad sheets littered the ground. Every so often someone stopped her and asked her to scan a QR code to follow a WeChat account.

Zheng Hai had left Neijiang, Sichuan two days earlier. He and his parents rode a train for 30 hours to reach Beijing. "It's so big, and the traffic is so bad. The air isn't as bad as I imagined," he said of his first impression of the city. After waiting an hour at the station, he boarded a school bus to the Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT) campus in Haidian District, where more than 3,000 new undergraduates would register.

While students waited for school buses, merchants' own buses, plastered with huge ads for Meizu, Acer and Didi, shuttled around the train station. The merchants didn't want to miss a single chance to reach a new student, and for the many students from out of town, the station is the first point of contact.

![A Meizu welcome bus for new students](http://cms.qdaily.com/uploads/image/201509/b342a8fe25e5.jpg)

Meizu says it ran welcome buses at nearly 40 universities in Beijing, Xi'an, Jinan, Chongqing and Changsha, carrying freshmen from train stations to campus, with free Wi-Fi and drinking water on board. Didi also ran free welcome buses in Beijing for several schools, including Renmin University of China and Peking University. It was Didi's first back-to-school campaign; until then it had believed that handing out red envelopes was enough to reach every group.

Along this fairly short main road, ad banners, printed posters and roll-up stands were everywhere. China Mobile had even hired people in mascot costumes.

![Advertising stalls on campus](/uploads/image/201509/67014db8c9de.jpg)Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

![Banners and roll-up stands along the main road](/uploads/image/201509/1e7b7328abb7.jpg)

A giant ad for ChinaHR hung over the sports field. A roll-up stand beside the China Construction Bank booth read "Dragon Card Elite University Card: the credit calling card that takes BUPT people around the world." A joint poster for China Telecom and Yihaodian stood not far from one for China Unicom and Linglinghua...

After finishing the formalities, Zheng Hai took another school bus 28 kilometers to BUPT's Changping campus, where he sat through another round of sales pitches. He hardly agonized over a SIM card, though. A China Unicom staffer told him Unicom had the best signal in Changping, so he signed up. Lu Wenwen didn't need a SIM card, but she got a Shanghai Pudong Development Bank card, because signing up came with a lunch box and a water cup, and she happened to have forgotten her cup that day.

If the stall staff hadn't been shouting, Lu Wenwen might never have noticed the Pudong Development Bank salesperson. There were no posters or signs for the bank, because it was China Mobile's booth. Usually, once the China Mobile staff finished their pitch, the Pudong Development Bank people stepped in and spread out their brochures: "Want a card? It turns straight into a credit card when you graduate."

### I

National policy places many limits on credit cards for university students. Even the card Lu Wenwen got needs a parent's guarantee before it carries a credit limit. She plans to use it as a debit card linked to Taobao for shopping. Her tuition card had already arrived from the school with her admission letter, issued by the Agricultural Bank of China. At Fudan University, 5 kilometers away, the longest line on the first day of term was also at the Agricultural Bank's card-opening point.

For the four big state-owned banks (ICBC, ABC, BOC and CCB), the tuition card, which the banks call the campus card, is the campus business they must win, and usually where they fight hardest. "At every bank, the campus card is top priority," an ICBC employee told QDaily. "In campus business, banks aren't counting on students' deposits. It's mainly about running up the number of cards opened and online-banking sign-ups, a showcase project for performance reviews. It used to be strongly encouraged, but competition keeps getting fiercer, and school policy restrictions make it harder and harder."

"China Merchants Bank doesn't do much with campus cards. The big four have them all locked up," said a corporate-banking account manager at China Merchants Bank. "Business with schools needs government approval. Each new set of leaders brings a new policy, and without connections, a school won't easily switch cards."

But other banks have found other ways onto campus. The "0-yuan credit card" that Zhima Credit and China Merchants Bank recently promoted together has no overdraft limit: you have to deposit money before you can spend. But spending records from the university years can serve as a credit history when the student applies for a credit card after graduation.

"Banks trust us more and more now. The benefit is that through these services, university students can hope to become independent earlier, with opportunities such as credit loans and part-time work," said Shen Haoxiang, head of Zhima Credit's "University Student Credit Festival." "The banks had no way to reach people with no credit record, and we can give them some initial data."

JD Baitiao, another product built on spending ahead of income, also values this opportunity. Before freshmen reached campus, it was already working closely with EMS and telecom carriers to give incoming students credit limits, and it tried launching credit-based internship and startup programs over the summer break.

"The campus market is still a small share of JD's total, but for JD the campus represents the future. Through a range of services during the university years, JD hopes students will come to know and accept the JD brand, not just while they're in school, but for the next 10 to 20 years," JD told QDaily.

Following the carriers onto campus is another, second-best option.

In 2014, Pudong Development Bank was already setting up stalls with China Mobile, each drawing customers for the other, which also put pressure on other carriers' stalls. Freshmen want credit cards much less than they want carrier services, so banks prefer to team up with carriers: once freshmen finish their phone business, they might glance at the credit card offer too. A person familiar with the matter said Pudong Development Bank issued about 800 credit cards on campuses this year.

![A Renrenfenqi stand at a parcel pickup point](http://cms.qdaily.com/uploads/image/201509/4536b6f7fed5.jpg)

Renrenfenqi, at the parcel pickup point of the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

Internet finance companies have also set their sights on university students. "Financial products like Fenqile and Jiedaibao are now the main sponsors the student union goes after," said Wang Haolin of the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, who used to handle sponsorship outreach at his school. He recently bought a Casio solar quartz watch on Fenqile, to be paid off in 18 installments. "I was planning to get one anyway, and an interest-free promotion happened to be running at the start of term."

### II

He has also noticed more and more phone brands trying to take over campuses. In August, Luo Yonghao, founder of Smartisan, announced that the company's new budget line, "Jianguo" (Nut), would team up with Fenqile, an installment-payment platform aimed at young people, on a 12-month interest-free phone plan. A monthly payment of 75 yuan is an amount nearly any university student can manage. "Students who work their way through school to buy a phone are proud young people by nature," he said. While Xiaomi, Meizu and other makers cut prices for the back-to-school season, Luo Yonghao hoped this approach would win over more hesitant student buyers.

But competitors had prepared long before. OPPO began planning in May, with the goal that "OPPO must be seen all over the country," focusing on key universities in first- and second-tier cities. "The back-to-school season is an important point in our annual marketing plan," Gu Yanyan, OPPO's campus promotion manager, told QDaily. OPPO takes part in everything from welcoming freshmen to sponsoring freshman galas.

In the second half of 2014, Meizu set up a dedicated campus marketing team. "For Meizu, the back-to-school season isn't only a campus marketing opportunity, but a way to get closer to young people." Meizu says that this season it will market online and offline at more than 200 universities nationwide. It also placed ads in the freshman handbooks of 50 universities.

Compared with the post-1980s generation, the post-1990s generation is often called "native" to phones: phones have been part of their lives since childhood. Most of this year's freshmen were born around 1997, the year phones are considered to have gone mainstream in China. Users grew from 48,000 in 1991 to 10 million that year, and growth then took off: by the end of 2002 there were 266 million.

So the post-1990s generation also wants novelty in digital products, values standing out, loves internet culture and cares about experience. "That's why we hold product trial events and enthusiast meetups on campus, and in marketing we also promote our products by partnering with the phone apps young people like," Meizu said.

Drawing on its marketing experience in this market, Meizu launched the "Meilan" brand in late 2014, designed to suit young people and positioned as "Quality For Young." According to Meizu, the Meilan brand passed 5 million units in total sales five months after launch; the Meilan note2, released this June, sold 1.2 million units in July alone. "At every product launch, many Meizu fans still in school turn up on their own to cheer us on. That has everything to do with how much attention Meizu has always paid to the campus market."

OPPO, for its part, launched its latest flagship, the R7, for the back-to-school season, with a slogan broadcast again and again: "Five minutes of charging, two hours of talk time." "This also speaks to the post-1990s mindset of 'I want it, and I want it now,'" Gu Yanyan said.

### III

Ding Haoyuan, from Shanxi, is a freshman at East China University of Science and Technology. After two bad airport meals and a cafeteria's cloyingly sweet braised pork, he was desperate to find a bowl of his hometown's pickled-cabbage-and-shredded-pork hele noodles on the snack street by the school's north side gate.

Before coming to Shanghai, he had never heard of the drink brand Suntory and had never ordered food delivery. His phone had no ordering apps such as Meituan or Ele.me.

Like Ding Haoyuan, Chen Xuyi of Shanghai International Studies University had no food-ordering apps on her phone before university. "My mom is a doctor, and she thought restaurant food was unhealthy." But by her third year she was used to ordering on her phone. "When my noon class ends I place an order, and by the time I walk back to the dorm the food has just arrived. At 8 or 9 in the evening I'll also order West Lake beef soup or chicken noodle soup as a late-night snack. It's way cuter than instant noodles."

Without noticing, university students are having their spending habits and ways of life changed and formed. Waiting downstairs for a delivery has become a signature scene of dorm life.

Senior Yang Yunyan uses Ele.me every day. "So do my roommates. From what I see around me, Ele.me and Meituan are the delivery apps university students use most. For one thing, it's convenient. Eating out is crowded, and the school cafeteria is packed and not very good."

Besides the "craving" for convenience, there is the lure of promotions, which are often merchants' main weapon in winning over students.

Before university, Hang Jiahao used only Dianping. After starting university he downloaded Ele.me, and when Ele.me's discounts shrank, he installed Meituan. When he activated online banking in his second year, he downloaded the ICBC banking app. When he bought movie tickets just for himself, he didn't care about seats together or prices; once he had a girlfriend, he downloaded Gewara. As he made more friends at university, he couldn't remember all their birthdays, so he downloaded Birthday Manager... Now a senior, Hang Jiahao crosses most of the city three days a week, shuttling between his internship and the university town. To pass the hour-and-a-half ride, he downloaded PPTV to watch movies on the way.

This is probably the path most freshmen's app collections will follow. It may also trace the progress of their university lives and their spending, and it is why merchants put so much effort into back-to-school marketing for freshmen.

Meituan also handed out "back-to-school gift packs" at major universities across the country this year, filled with vouchers for its range of products, in the hope of capturing students', especially freshmen's, spending on "eating, drinking and fun."

Compared with the past, university students spend more on hotels and travel. Demand for hotel stays near campus and short trips nearby is growing especially fast: students pulling all-nighters to study, students in dorms without air conditioning renting rooms nearby in the summer heat, couples renting rooms, class outings. These are markets not yet fully tapped.

A Meituan employee told QDaily that university students are very price-sensitive, and campaigns aimed at them, such as exam-cramming room specials and summer short-trip deals, tend to sell well.

"Over the next three years, demand for campus advertising will certainly rise, because students' spending power keeps growing, and so does their openness to new ideas. Demand exceeds supply, so this market is bound to do well," said Xiong Wenjun, media director at PMG Feizhuo Media Group. The company is currently the largest agency for campus light-box advertising, covering about 500 universities across China.

Junior Yu Yayun barely remembers the hard-sell ads on campus. "I usually can't be bothered to look at hard promotions. And with the promotions that ask you to follow a WeChat account, I basically unfollow once the event is over." What stayed with her was Cornetto, the sponsor of her school's Top Ten Singers contest. "They handed out balloons and ice cream, and everyone loved it. We can be bought with little freebies. Lots of merchants just don't get us."

### IV

Guo Yue finally chose China Mobile, mainly because topping up 300 yuan of phone credit got you a free bicycle. A Phoenix bicycle salesman with a stall at Songjiang University Town said business is best in September, and on his best day he can sell more than a hundred bikes. In 2013, China Telecom ordered 50,000 bicycles from Forever for promotions. Forever never expected them to sell so well, and even had to ask Phoenix's manufacturer for more stock. The salesman used to set up his stall on campus too, but for the past two years he hasn't been allowed in.

In back-to-school marketing, the loudest players are usually the three carriers, China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom, and the competition among them is also the fiercest.

![China Unicom notice board for international students](http://cms.qdaily.com/uploads/image/201509/f91813e6c790.jpg)

A notice board China Unicom prepared for international students

At Fudan University, China Mobile stalls were all over campus. On the road from the registration point to the textbook pickup point, at least 8 sales reps were pressing tote bags and fans printed with China Mobile ads on passing students. Giant posters for Tianyi Broadband and 4G stood out brightly at the basketball court, and outside the supermarket a sign on a utility pole pointed the way to China Telecom.

Jiang Cheng joined China Mobile last year and used to handle back-to-school marketing for northern Shanghai. He said preparation for welcoming freshmen usually starts three months ahead, including counting heads and producing materials. On arrival day, the team has to be at the school by five or six in the morning to put up tents and set up stalls. By eight or nine, freshmen start trickling onto campus.

![A joint China Telecom and Huawei stall](http://cms.qdaily.com/uploads/image/201509/a645c627e857.jpg)

A joint China Telecom and Huawei project

Compared with regular retail plans, the three carriers' freshman plans come with deep discounts, sometimes even a free monthly fee for the first year, all to win the freshman market.

"But overall, the three carriers can't afford a destructive price war with big gaps between them. Everyone's offers are about the same," Jiang Cheng told a QDaily reporter.

So being first, or even the only carrier, to cover a school's network becomes a big advantage. Bundling SIM cards with broadband as buy-one-get-one deals also appeals strongly to students. When China Telecom chooses which campuses to enter, it focuses on schools its resources already reach, including fiber broadband, Wi-Fi and 4G.

According to China Telecom, it currently provides about 70% of university Wi-Fi service. This year it entered 2,974 universities nationwide, including 68 in Shanghai and 130 in Beijing.

As smartphones spread, post-1990s students need more data and less talk time, and they have moved from paying at business halls to paying online. China Telecom has responded by shifting its marketing focus from voice and text messages to data and Wi-Fi, and by switching plans from monthly to annual payment for convenience. This year, for example, it launched a plan of 400 yuan for 2 years, with no monthly fee on the 2-year bill. Payment has moved from business halls to online. China Mobile and China Unicom have made much the same changes.

### V

How important is the campus market to brands? The question is almost the same as "How important is the post-1990s generation to brands?" Nearly every company QDaily interviewed for this story used words like "very important."

According to a 2014 report from the market research firm Nielsen, the "broad post-1990s" cohort, those born between 1985 and 1995, made up 17% of China's population and contributed 15% of total consumer spending. But Nielsen expects the group's large spending potential to lift that share sharply, to 35%, by 2020.

That includes post-1990s students who haven't graduated yet and in theory have no income. According to the Ministry of Education's university enrollment plan, there will be nearly 7 million new university students this year, and more than 30 million undergraduates enrolled.

These students' purchasing power can't be ignored either. As society as a whole has grown richer, whether the money comes from parents or part-time jobs, the cash students have to spend is growing year by year. Among the freshmen QDaily interviewed, a girl from Yantai, Shandong got 2,000 yuan in pocket money from her parents for her first month, and a boy who flew to Shanghai from Chongqing gets as much as 9,000 yuan for a single semester.

Before students' spending habits are formed, brands have also begun to grasp that they buy on impulse and spend ahead of income. In 2013, more than 55% of students in China were already shopping online, spending over 4,000 yuan a year on average. And in 2015, Huabei, a small-loan service tied closely to Alipay, announced that one-third of its users were post-1990s.

The way brands chase these young people tells you that they expect the group's spending power to grow even stronger.

Apple's back-to-school promotion this year offered not only an education discount (still expensive after the cut), and Apple also hoped to throw in a pair of equally expensive Beats headphones with each computer it sold.

Acer also told QDaily that it will drop its old "value for money" approach and make distinctive, high-spec products for students who can afford them.

Another important change in Acer's back-to-school marketing this year is a shift in focus to ordinary, non-elite universities in second- to fourth-tier cities, including vocational and technical colleges, places that have drawn little public attention or merchant interest in the past. The outside reason is that "211" and "985" universities are run more strictly and make harsh demands on merchants and companies. The inside reason is Acer's need to grow in the campus market and push its sales channels into smaller cities.

### VI

Brands all covet these young people in their twenties, whose spending power is nearly matched by their impulsiveness. But the campus market is unusual, and brands have only started to push into it faster in recent years. In this process, reaching campus consumers early may be one of the most important factors.

Take the bank card and SIM card that arrive with your admission letter. They come from the traditional companies that have worked the campus longest: carriers like China Mobile and China Unicom, or the big state-owned banks. These companies often have relationships with schools going back decades, and they carry that advantage to every new class of students.

![The "carrier war" at a Shanghai university](http://cms.qdaily.com/uploads/image/201509/d33ec89a07cd.jpg)

The "carrier war" at the University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

Because these services are tied to scholarships, campus cards or class text-message notices, you may not give them up until you graduate. But most of these bundled services are undoubtedly terrible to use. You may find, for example, that the online-banking payment limit on the card your school gave you won't even let you pay your tuition in one day.

But as these "national-level" giants need to grow and expand their core businesses, they are starting to compete with each other. China Mobile, China Unicom and China Telecom are all using 4G plans to win users, and China Telecom's lead in the traditional campus broadband market may be challenged by China Unicom in future.

Banks are the same. Beyond the default bank card every student holds, it is already common for students to open other accounts to stash private savings or to invest. That leaves room to grow for banks such as China Merchants Bank and China Construction Bank, which traditionally can't go onto campus to do business directly.

A typical case is Pudong Development Bank, mentioned earlier, or the makers of carrier-contract phones. It followed one of the campus market's monopolists onto campus and doesn't dare to push its own business openly. But when it gets the chance, it is still closer to students than companies that have to build their brands from scratch off campus.

For companies without a head start, winning student consumers takes steady, long-term guidance in their daily lives. That means bigger everyday brand marketing, and more effort. The drink ads in campus light boxes, the endless food-delivery red envelopes, the charity sales cosmetics companies hold on campus, the big brand-sponsored campus events: all of these belong in this category.

Compared with arriving at school, when there was no time to choose, in theory students now have sharper judgment: they can compare prices across three apps before ordering food, or simply ignore the promotions. But brands don't see it that way. More merchants care about students' future habits and buying decisions than about the present.

Consumer psychologist Martin Lindstrom has said that when we are about to make a purchase, the brain recalls and scans countless memories, facts and emotions, and compresses them into a quick reaction. That kind of "burst" is exactly what brands that failed to catch your eye at the start are after.

At the end of the day, Zheng Hai summed up his first day in one word: "Tired." After a string of enrollment procedures, Lu Wenwen also felt more worn out than excited. They may not have noticed the countless other ads on campus that day with designs on them (including QDaily's own light-box ads). "If the deal had been signed three days later, there'd have been no spot left for QDaily," Xiong Wenjun said.

"A campus is a small society. If a brand wants to reach more men, it picks spots like sports fields; for women, the usual choice is libraries, paths and so on," Xiong Wenjun said. Because the Ministry of Education has banned obvious advertising from campuses, advertisers find other ways in, such as putting ads on first-aid kits. Cosmetics, drinks, education companies and game companies are among the main categories advertising on campuses.

Term has begun and freshmen have started military training, but the giant posters and light-box ads scattered across campus are still up, and commerce carries on at school.

(At the interviewees' request, all students in this article are identified by pseudonyms.)
